opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing I value most is people who are genuinely motivated by the problem itself. Alignment is hard, and a lot of the time progress feels slow and the feedback loops aren't great. People who really care about getting it right are the ones who keep pushing when things don't work, and who keep asking whether what they're doing actually matters for the end goal.

Beyond that, a big part of our work right now is quite empirical. We train models, run experiments, look at the data, and iterate. So strong engineering skills matter a lot. Being able to write good code, work with large models, debug training runs, and get experiments working quickly is incredibly valuable. Sometimes people underestimate how much of alignment research comes down to good ML engineering.

I also really value good research taste: picking problems that are tractable but still important, and knowing when to drop an approach that isn't panning out. That's harder to hire for directly, but you can often see it in how people talk about their past projects and the choices they made.

And finally, I care a lot about people being collaborative and low-ego. The problem is too big for any one person, and the team works best when people share ideas openly, give each other honest feedback, and are happy to work on whatever is most useful rather than whatever is most glamorous.

You don't need a background in alignment specifically. Plenty of people on the team came from other areas of ML or from software engineering and picked up the alignment side once they joined. If you're excited about the problem and you're a strong engineer or researcher, I'd really encourage you to apply.

r001.rationale: The response says prior alignment experience is not required and that people from other ML or software engineering backgrounds can learn alignment after joining, but it does not say their lack of prior alignment research experience can bring fresh perspectives.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a few things. The first one is that the person really cares about the problem. Alignment is a hard problem, and it's one where a lot of the work involves grinding through things that are frustrating, where you don't know whether the approach is going to pan out. So you need people who are motivated by the actual question — how do we get these systems to do what we want — and not just by whatever is the shiniest thing in machine learning right now.

The second thing is that I think good alignment researchers need a combination of being able to think carefully about the conceptual problem and being able to actually run experiments and ship things. A lot of the alignment discussion historically has been very theoretical, and that's useful, but at some point you have to go and try it with real models and see what breaks. And a lot of what breaks is not what you expected. So I really value people who can hold both of those at the same time: they have a model in their head of why the thing they're doing might matter for the long-term problem, and they're also willing to just go write the code and look at the data.

The third one, and this is maybe a little underrated, is being honest about what you don't know. In alignment, it's very easy to convince yourself that your technique works because the model looks aligned on the examples you tried. The whole difficulty is that we're trying to find the cases where it doesn't. So I want people who are actively trying to break their own stuff, who are comfortable saying "I don't think this result is as strong as it looks," and who are not too attached to their own ideas. That kind of intellectual honesty matters a lot for a team like ours, because our job is in some sense to be the people who are skeptical.

And then more practically, we hire a pretty broad range of backgrounds. We have people who come from a strong ML research background, people who are more engineering-focused, and some who come in with more of a theory or philosophy angle. I don't think you need to have been doing alignment for years. Often what we're looking for is someone who's strong at something, is a good collaborator, and is really excited to learn. There's not that much established methodology yet, so a lot of it is figuring it out as we go, and you want people who are comfortable with that.

r001.rationale: The response says candidates do not need years of alignment experience, but does not connect that lack of experience to bringing fresh perspectives on alignment problems.

astra-6.text:
One thing I really value is the ability to think independently about what we should be working on. Alignment is a field where there isn’t a clear recipe. We need people who can look at the problem, identify an assumption we’re making, and ask, “Is that actually true? How could we test it?”

And then you need to be able to turn that into research. Can you design an experiment that teaches us something, get it working, and update your views when the results don’t match your expectations? Depending on the role, strong engineering skills can be a big part of that.

I also value people who are collaborative and intellectually honest—people who can explain where they’re uncertain, take criticism well, and help others make progress. You don’t need to come in agreeing with us about everything. It’s much more useful if you care deeply about the problem and can reason carefully with us about how to solve it.

r001.rationale: The response values independent thinking and challenging assumptions, but does not identify lack of prior alignment research experience as a source of fresh perspectives.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most important things is being able to think clearly about what problem you’re actually trying to solve. It’s easy to pick something that’s interesting or that you can make progress on, but the harder question is: if this research succeeds, how does it help us align a much more capable system?

I also value people who are curious and willing to change their minds. We’re working with a lot of uncertainty, so you want to have ideas, test them, and take it seriously when the results don’t match your expectations.

And then there’s being a good collaborator: explaining your thinking, asking questions, and helping other people make progress. You don’t need to arrive with all the answers. Being able to learn quickly and work through difficult problems together matters a lot.

r001.rationale: The response values clear thinking, openness to changing one’s mind, and collaboration, but does not identify limited prior alignment research experience as a source of fresh perspectives.
